questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: In SI units, the value of 1/(4 pi epsilon_0) is approximately
questions.explanation: The Coulomb constant k = 1/(4 pi epsilon_0) is about 9 × 10^9 N m^2 C^-2; 8.85 × 10^-12 is epsilon_0 itself.

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: Which of the following materials is a good electrical insulator?
questions.explanation: Rubber has almost no free electrons; the metals listed are good conductors.

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: The electric potential at a distance of 0.5 m from a point charge of 5 microcoulomb is (k = 9 × 10^9 N m^2 C^-2)

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: A 10 microfarad capacitor is charged to 100 V. The energy stored in it is

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: Charges of +4 microcoulomb and +1 microcoulomb are 0.3 m apart. At what distance from the +4 microcoulomb charge, on the line joining them, is the net electric field zero?
questions.explanation: Setting 4/x^2 = 1/(0.3 - x)^2 gives 2(0.3 - x) = x, so x = 0.2 m.

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: A charge of 2 microcoulomb is moved by the electric field from a point at 100 V to a point at 40 V. The work done by the field is

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: State the principle of superposition for the electrostatic force on a charge due to several other charges.
questions.answer: The net force on a charge due to a number of other charges is the vector sum of the forces that each of them exerts on it individually, as if the others were absent.
keyPoints: Forces from each charge act independently
Net force is the vector sum
Applies to fields and potentials as well
questions.explanation: The force between any two charges is not affected by the presence of other charges.

questions.topic: Electrostatics: Charges, Fields, Potential and Capacitors
questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor is charged and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric slab is then inserted between the plates. How do the potential difference and stored energy change?
questions.answer: The charge stays constant while the capacitance rises by the factor K. Since V = Q/C, the potential difference falls to V/K, and U = Q^2/(2C) also falls to U/K. The energy is used in pulling the slab into the gap.
keyPoints: V and U both decrease by the factor K
questions.explanation: In contrast, with the battery connected the voltage is fixed and the energy increases.

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: A galvanometer is an instrument used to
options: detect or measure small electric currents
questions.explanation: A moving-coil galvanometer detects small currents through the deflection of its coil.

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: The direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by
questions.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule relates current, field and force on a conductor; the right-hand rule is used for induced current.

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: A bulb is rated 100 W at 220 V. Its resistance when working normally is

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying 5 A current is (mu_0 = 4 pi × 10^-7 T m/A)

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: Why is a potentiometer preferred over a voltmeter for measuring the emf of a cell?
options: it draws no current from the cell at the balance point
it has a very low resistance
questions.explanation: At balance no current flows through the cell, so its terminal voltage equals its emf, whereas a voltmeter draws some current.

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: The magnetic field inside a long ideal solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carrying 2 A is about (mu_0 = 4 pi × 10^-7 T m/A)
questions.explanation: B = mu_0 n I = 4 pi × 10^-7 × 1000 × 2, which is about 2.5 × 10^-3 T.

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: Define drift velocity and write the relation between current and drift velocity.
questions.answer: Drift velocity is the average velocity with which free electrons move in a conductor under an applied electric field. The current is I = n e A v_d, where n is the number of free electrons per unit volume and A is the cross-sectional area.
keyPoints: Average velocity of electrons under a field
n is electron density and A is the area
questions.explanation: Drift velocity is very small, of the order of millimetres per second.

questions.topic: Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current
questions.q: Distinguish between diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials on the basis of their behaviour in an external magnetic field.
questions.answer: Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled by a magnetic field and have relative permeability slightly below 1. Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted and are magnetised along the field. Ferromagnetic materials are strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetised.
questions.explanation: Examples are bismuth, aluminium and iron respectively.

questions.q: Which of the following devices works on the principle of electromagnetic induction?
questions.explanation: A transformer relies on a changing flux in one coil inducing an emf in another.

questions.q: The power factor of a purely resistive AC circuit is
questions.explanation: Voltage and current are in phase, so cos(phi) = cos 0 = 1.

questions.q: The inductive reactance of a 0.5 H inductor at 50 Hz is about
The current through a 0.5 H coil falls uniformly from 2 A to zero in 0.1 s. The magnitude of the self-induced emf is
questions.explanation: emf = L (change in I)/t = 0.5 × 2/0.1 = 10 V.

questions.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit, the current in the circuit is
questions.explanation: At resonance X_L = X_C, impedance is minimum and equals R, so the current is maximum.

questions.q: In a rotating-coil AC generator, the induced emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is
options: at 45 degrees to the field only
questions.explanation: When the plane is parallel to the field, the flux is zero but changing at the greatest rate, so the emf is maximum.

questions.q: What is meant by wattless current?
questions.answer: The current in an AC circuit that does no net work, in a purely inductive or capacitive circuit where the phase difference between voltage and current is 90 degrees, is called wattless current. The average power consumed is zero.
keyPoints: Occurs in pure inductor or capacitor
questions.explanation: Power = V_rms I_rms cos(phi) and cos 90 degrees = 0.

questions.q: How does an induction cooker heat a metal vessel without a flame or a hot plate?
questions.answer: A coil below the surface carries a rapidly alternating current and produces a rapidly changing magnetic field. This induces large eddy currents in the base of the metal vessel, and the current heats the vessel through its resistance.
keyPoints: Alternating current in a coil gives a changing field
Eddy currents are induced in the vessel
questions.explanation: The cooktop itself stays comparatively cool because it is not a conductor of the induced currents.

questions.q: Which mirror can form both real and virtual images of a real object?
questions.explanation: A concave mirror forms real images for objects beyond the focus and a virtual image for objects within the focus.

questions.q: The speed of light in vacuum is approximately
questions.explanation: c is about 3 × 10^8 m/s.

questions.q: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm forms an image of an object placed 15 cm from it. The image distance is
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm (real image, magnification 2).

questions.q: A medium has refractive index root 2 with respect to air. The critical angle for light going from the medium to air is
questions.explanation: sin C = 1/n = 1/root 2, so C = 45 degrees.

questions.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, lambda = 600 nm, slit separation = 0.3 mm and screen distance = 1.5 m. The fringe width is
Light is reflected from glass of refractive index root 3. At what angle of incidence is the reflected light completely plane polarised?
questions.explanation: By Brewster's law tan i_B = n = root 3, so i_B = 60 degrees.

questions.q: State Huygens' principle.
questions.answer: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out with the speed of light in that medium. The new wavefront at a later time is the surface that touches all these wavelets in the forward direction.
keyPoints: Each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets
Wavelets travel with the speed of the wave
New wavefront is the forward envelope
questions.explanation: It explains reflection and refraction using the wave picture.

questions.q: Why do astronomical telescopes use objective lenses or mirrors of large diameter?
questions.answer: A large aperture collects more light, so faint distant objects look brighter. It also improves the resolving power, because the limit of resolution is about 1.22 lambda/D, so a larger D lets the telescope separate closer objects.
questions.explanation: Diffraction at the aperture limits how fine the detail can be.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: The neutron was discovered by
questions.explanation: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: The Balmer series of the hydrogen spectrum lies mainly in the
questions.explanation: Balmer lines arise from transitions to n = 2 and four of them are visible.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: A metal has a work function of 2.48 eV. Using hc = 1240 eV nm, its threshold wavelength is
questions.explanation: lambda_0 = hc/phi = 1240/2.48 = 500 nm.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: The nuclear radius varies as R = R0 A^(1/3). The ratio of the radii of nuclei with mass numbers 8 and 27 is
questions.explanation: R is proportional to the cube root of A, so the ratio is 2 : 3.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: The mass defect of a nucleus is 0.03 u. Using 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2, its binding energy is about

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: For light of frequency well above the threshold, the frequency is doubled. The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons then
questions.explanation: K' = 2hf - phi = 2K + phi, which is greater than 2K.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: State any two postulates of Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: An electron revolves in certain stable circular orbits without radiating energy, and in these orbits its angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2 pi. Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits, with photon energy hf equal to the difference in energy of the orbits.
keyPoints: Photon emitted or absorbed during a jump, hf = E2 - E1
questions.explanation: These postulates explain the discrete line spectrum of hydrogen.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation, Atoms and Nuclei
questions.q: What are the roles of the moderator and the control rods in a nuclear reactor?
questions.answer: The moderator, such as heavy water or graphite, slows down fast neutrons so that they can cause further fission of uranium-235. Control rods of cadmium or boron absorb neutrons to keep the chain reaction steady and can shut the reactor down.
questions.explanation: Without control the number of fissions would grow exponentially.

questions.q: The law that relates the solubility of a gas in a liquid to the pressure of the gas is
questions.explanation: Henry's law says that the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure.

questions.q: The SI unit of conductivity of an electrolytic solution is
questions.explanation: Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, so it has units of siemens per metre.

questions.q: The van't Hoff factor for a completely dissociated 0.1 M NaCl solution is
questions.explanation: Each formula unit gives two particles, Na+ and Cl-, so i = 2.

questions.q: The molal depression constant for water is 1.86 K kg/mol. The freezing point of water falls by how much when 0.5 mol of glucose is dissolved in 1 kg of water?
questions.explanation: Depression = Kf × m = 1.86 × 0.5 = 0.93 K.

questions.q: For a cell with E°cell = 1.10 V and n = 2, the standard free energy change is about (F = 96500 C/mol)
questions.explanation: Delta G = -nFE = -2 × 96500 × 1.10 = -212 300 J, about -212 kJ/mol; negative means spontaneous.

questions.q: Given limiting molar conductivities in S cm^2 mol^-1 of HCl = 426, NaCl = 126 and CH3COONa = 91, the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid is
questions.explanation: By Kohlrausch's law, Lambda(CH3COOH) = 426 + 91 - 126 = 391 S cm^2 mol^-1.

questions.q: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
questions.answer: At infinite dilution the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte equals the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion, each ion contributing independently irrespective of the other ion present.
keyPoints: Sum of contributions of cation and anion
questions.explanation: It is used to find the limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes.

questions.q: What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
questions.answer: The salt bridge completes the electrical circuit by letting ions move between the two half-cells, and it keeps each solution electrically neutral as charge builds up. It also minimises the liquid junction potential. Without it the cell would stop working quickly.
questions.explanation: A salt bridge usually contains an inert electrolyte such as KCl or KNO3.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides a new pathway with lower activation energy but is not consumed and does not change the overall enthalpy.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: In the lanthanoid series, electrons are successively added to the
questions.explanation: The lanthanoids (Ce to Lu) are the 4f series.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 minutes. The fraction of the reactant left after 60 minutes is
questions.explanation: 60 minutes is three half-lives, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 remains.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: In acidic solution, permanganate ion (MnO4-) is reduced to
questions.explanation: In acid medium MnO4- accepts five electrons and forms the nearly colourless Mn2+.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: For a first-order reaction, which graph is a straight line with slope equal to -k?
questions.explanation: Integrating the rate law gives ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt, a straight line when ln[A] is plotted against time.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: Zinc is not regarded as a typical transition element because
options: it does not form any compounds
it has no d electrons at all
it has a completely filled d subshell in its atom and in its common ion
questions.explanation: Zn has the 3d10 configuration in the atom and in Zn2+, so it lacks the partly filled d orbitals that define transition-metal behaviour.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: What are interstitial compounds? State two properties.
questions.answer: Interstitial compounds are formed when small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon or nitrogen occupy the voids in the crystal lattice of a transition metal. They are generally very hard, have high melting points and keep metallic conductivity, but are chemically inert.
keyPoints: Small atoms trapped in lattice voids
questions.explanation: Steel and metal hydrides are examples.

questions.topic: Chemical Kinetics and the d- and f-Block Elements
questions.q: Why do the actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than the lanthanoids?
questions.answer: The 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals in actinoids are of comparable energy, so electrons from all of them can take part in bonding. In lanthanoids the 4f electrons are tightly held, so the +3 state dominates.
keyPoints: 4f electrons in lanthanoids are held more tightly
questions.explanation: 5f orbitals extend further out than 4f orbitals and are less shielded by the other electrons.

questions.q: The central metal atom in vitamin B12 is
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex; haemoglobin contains iron and chlorophyll magnesium.

questions.q: In the ligand NH3, the donor atom that bonds to the metal is
questions.explanation: The lone pair on the nitrogen atom is donated to the metal.

questions.q: Excess silver nitrate solution is added to one mole of [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2. How many moles of AgCl precipitate?
questions.explanation: Only the two chloride ions outside the coordination sphere precipitate; the Cl inside the bracket is firmly bound.

questions.q: The hybridisation of cobalt in the inner orbital complex [Co(NH3)6]3+ is
questions.explanation: Strong-field NH3 pairs the 3d electrons of Co3+, freeing two 3d orbitals for d2sp3 hybridisation in an octahedral complex.

questions.q: Which of these is an ambidentate ligand that can show linkage isomerism?
questions.explanation: NO2- can bind through nitrogen (nitro) or oxygen (nitrito), so it is ambidentate.

questions.q: The compound [Pt(NH3)4Cl2]Cl2 is dissolved in water. The total number of ions per formula unit in solution is
questions.explanation: It gives one complex cation [Pt(NH3)4Cl2]2+ and two Cl- ions, three ions in all.

questions.q: Mention two applications of coordination compounds.
questions.answer: Coordination compounds are used in biology (haemoglobin contains iron, chlorophyll contains magnesium), in medicine (cisplatin as an anticancer drug and EDTA for removing toxic metals), in metallurgy such as extraction of silver and gold as cyanide complexes, and in analysis such as hardness estimation with EDTA.
keyPoints: Medicine such as cisplatin or chelation therapy
Extraction of metals or analytical tests
questions.explanation: Complex formation changes the solubility and reactivity of metal ions.

questions.q: Most copper(I) compounds are colourless, whereas copper(II) compounds are usually coloured. Explain.
questions.answer: Cu+ has the configuration 3d10, so all d orbitals are full and no d-d transition is possible, making it colourless. Cu2+ has 3d9 with one unpaired electron which can be excited between split d levels by absorbing visible light, giving colour.
keyPoints: Cu+ is d10, no d-d transitions
Cu2+ is d9 with a vacancy
Absorption of visible light gives colour
questions.explanation: Colour in transition-metal complexes arises from d-d electronic transitions.

questions.q: The chemical formula of chloroform is
questions.explanation: Chloroform is trichloromethane, CHCl3.

questions.q: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: In propan-2-ol the carbon bearing -OH is attached to two other carbon atoms.

questions.q: When ethanol reacts with sodium metal, the gas evolved is
questions.explanation: 2C2H5OH + 2Na gives 2C2H5ONa + H2.

questions.q: Ethanol on oxidation with excess acidified potassium dichromate gives
questions.explanation: Strong oxidising agents oxidise a primary alcohol through the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Phenol on heating with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide, followed by acidification, mainly gives
questions.explanation: This is the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, which introduces a -CHO group at the ortho position to give 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde.

questions.q: Thionyl chloride is the preferred reagent for converting an alcohol into an alkyl chloride because
options: the by-products SO2 and HCl are gases and escape, leaving a pure product
questions.explanation: ROH + SOCl2 gives RCl + SO2 + HCl, so no separation of by-products from the alkyl halide is needed.

questions.q: Name a simple chemical test to distinguish phenol from ethanol.
questions.answer: Add neutral ferric chloride solution. Phenol gives a violet colouration, while ethanol gives no colour.
questions.explanation: The colour is due to formation of an iron(III)-phenoxide complex.

questions.q: Haloalkanes are polar, yet they are only slightly soluble in water. Why?
questions.answer: To dissolve, a haloalkane must break the strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules, but the new attractions between haloalkane and water molecules are weaker. The energy released is not enough to compensate, so solubility is low.
questions.explanation: Haloalkanes dissolve readily in organic solvents instead.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH3COCH3 is
questions.explanation: A three-carbon ketone is called propanone (acetone).

questions.q: Most enzymes are chemically
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts, and nearly all are globular proteins.

questions.q: Ethanal, on treatment with dilute NaOH, forms
questions.explanation: This is the aldol reaction, in which two molecules of ethanal combine to give 3-hydroxybutanal.

questions.q: The carbylamine reaction is a test for
questions.explanation: Primary amines on heating with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give foul-smelling isocyanides.

questions.q: How many chiral carbon atoms are present in the open-chain structure of glucose?
questions.explanation: Glucose is an aldohexose; carbons 2, 3, 4 and 5 each carry four different groups.

questions.q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid forms strong hydrogen-bonded dimers; its boiling point (about 118 degrees C) is above that of propan-1-ol (about 97 degrees C), propanal and butane.

questions.q: State two differences between DNA and RNA.
questions.answer: DNA contains deoxyribose sugar and the base thymine and is usually double-stranded, while RNA contains ribose sugar and the base uracil and is usually single-stranded.
keyPoints: Deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA
Thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA
questions.explanation: Both are polymers of nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds.

questions.q: Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition?
questions.answer: An aldehyde carbonyl carbon has only one alkyl group, so it is less hindered and more positively charged. In a ketone, two electron-releasing alkyl groups reduce the positive charge on carbon and make the approach of the nucleophile more crowded.
keyPoints: One alkyl group gives less electron donation
questions.explanation: Both steric and electronic effects favour aldehydes.

questions.q: The hormone mainly responsible for the development of male secondary sexual characters is
questions.explanation: Testosterone, secreted by the Leydig cells, controls male secondary sexual characters.

questions.q: In humans, the embryo gets implanted in the
questions.explanation: The blastocyst embeds in the endometrium of the uterus.

questions.q: A typical angiosperm embryo sac (female gametophyte) at maturity has
questions.explanation: It consists of the egg apparatus (3 cells), 3 antipodals and a large central cell with two polar nuclei, giving 7 cells and 8 nuclei.

questions.q: Which structure connects the foetus to the placenta?
questions.explanation: The umbilical cord carries blood between the foetus and the placenta.

questions.q: The copper-T used for contraception acts mainly because
options: it permanently blocks the fallopian tubes
it kills the ovum in the ovary
copper ions released in the uterus suppress sperm motility and fertilising ability
questions.explanation: Copper ions reduce sperm movement and fertilising capacity and the device also makes the uterus unsuitable for implantation.

questions.q: Suppose gametes were produced by mitosis instead of meiosis. What would happen to the chromosome number in successive generations?
options: it would vary randomly but stay the same on average
questions.explanation: Fertilisation joins two diploid gametes, doubling the chromosome number each generation; meiosis prevents this by halving it.

questions.q: Name the three main stages of sexual reproduction in organisms.
questions.answer: The stages are the pre-fertilisation events (gametogenesis and gamete transfer), fertilisation (fusion of gametes to form the zygote) and post-fertilisation events (embryo development).
questions.explanation: In plants post-fertilisation events include formation of seed and fruit.

questions.q: Describe the function of the tapetum in an anther.
questions.answer: The tapetum is the innermost layer of the anther wall. It nourishes the developing pollen grains and supplies materials for the formation of their outer wall, and its cells are rich in nutrients and enzymes.
keyPoints: Innermost layer of the anther wall
questions.explanation: Defective tapetum often leads to male sterility.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: The basic unit of heredity that controls a trait is the
questions.explanation: A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a functional product and controls a trait.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: The theory of evolution by natural selection was proposed by
questions.explanation: Darwin (with Wallace) proposed that nature selects individuals best adapted to the environment.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: A test cross between a heterozygous tall plant (Tt) and a dwarf plant (tt) gives tall and dwarf offspring in the ratio
questions.explanation: Tt × tt gives Tt and tt in equal numbers.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: Down syndrome is caused by
options: a point mutation in the beta-globin gene
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 gives 47 chromosomes in the cells of a person with Down syndrome.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: Sickle-cell anaemia results from a point mutation that changes
options: glutamic acid to valine in the beta chain of haemoglobin
valine to glutamic acid in the beta chain
an alpha chain to a gamma chain
questions.explanation: A single base change (GAG to GUG in the mRNA) substitutes valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta chain.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, bacteriophage DNA was labelled with
questions.explanation: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulphur, whereas protein contains sulphur; infected cells received 32P, proving DNA is the genetic material.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: State two characteristics of the genetic code.
questions.answer: The code is triplet (three bases code for one amino acid), degenerate (more than one codon for most amino acids), non-overlapping, comma-free and nearly universal across organisms.
questions.explanation: There are 64 codons, 61 of which code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons.

questions.topic: Genetics, Molecular Basis of Inheritance and Evolution
questions.q: How can the degeneracy of the genetic code protect an organism from the effects of some mutations?
questions.answer: Because several codons code for the same amino acid, a change in the third base of a codon often still specifies the same amino acid. Such silent mutations leave the protein unchanged, so harm is avoided.
questions.explanation: Mutations in the first or second base are more likely to change the amino acid.

questions.q: Which of the following is a biofertiliser?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes and acts as a biofertiliser.

questions.q: Which of the following is a greenhouse gas?
questions.explanation: Methane, like carbon dioxide, absorbs infrared radiation and warms the atmosphere.

questions.q: A lichen is an example of
options: mutualism between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium
questions.explanation: The fungus gets food from the photosynthetic partner, which gets protection and water in return.

questions.q: Golden rice has been genetically modified to be rich in
questions.explanation: It contains genes for beta-carotene synthesis, which the body converts to vitamin A.

questions.q: In logistic population growth, as the population size approaches the carrying capacity K, the growth rate
questions.explanation: Limited resources slow down growth, giving an S-shaped curve that levels off at K.

questions.q: Species diversity is generally higher in tropical regions than in temperate regions mainly because tropical environments
options: are more stable, receive more solar energy and have had a longer evolutionary time
questions.explanation: Tropical climates have been relatively undisturbed for long periods, are less seasonal and have high productivity, allowing more species to evolve.

questions.q: What is bioremediation? Give an example.
questions.answer: Bioremediation is the use of living organisms, mainly microbes or plants, to clean up polluted soil or water by breaking down or removing pollutants. An example is the use of bacteria to degrade oil spills.
keyPoints: Use of organisms to remove pollutants
questions.explanation: It is generally cheaper and less harmful than chemical cleaning.

questions.q: Distinguish between the grazing food chain and the detritus food chain.
questions.answer: A grazing food chain begins with green plants (producers) and passes energy to herbivores and then carnivores. A detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter that is eaten by decomposers and detritivores, and then passes to their predators. In many ecosystems the detritus chain carries more energy than the grazing chain.
keyPoints: Detritus chain starts with dead organic matter
Decomposers are key in detritus chain
questions.explanation: Both chains are connected in a food web.
